events.summary: The PR author proposes shareable per-rule autofix control, continuing an earlier RFC and inviting feedback on an incomplete draft and implementation plan.
An automated CLA check records signed agreement status for the listed contributors.
The author challenges a claimed performance cost of object-shaped rule entries and offers a small benchmark, while acknowledging its limited realism.
A maintainer says the concern is retaining both array and object forms in memory and prefers a nonbreaking helper syntax backed by a separate autofix map.
The author revisits memory measurements and argues the overhead may be acceptable, while questioning how a top-level setting would interact with rule entries.
The maintainer reiterates that simultaneous internal representations, rather than either representation alone, are the concern; defineConfig could translate user syntax.
The author accepts the helper translation idea but asks which setting should win if both per-rule and top-level autofix declarations are allowed.
The maintainer suggests withholding top-level autofix from defineConfig initially, leaving lower-level configuration available to direct users.
The author asks whether helper-only syntax would remove proposed CLI and inline forms and how the design would cover linter option diagnostics.
A maintainer agrees that CLI and inline rule syntax would not gain the new setting under a helper-only approach.
Another maintainer favors a breaking object normalization because it would support future per-rule settings consistently across config, CLI, and inline directives.
The author supports object normalization and says waiting for a major release is preferable to a confusing compatibility workaround.
A maintainer asks the opposing maintainer whether the breaking design remains unacceptable.
The opposing maintainer says the narrow autofix use case does not justify changing the public rule configuration format.
A maintainer notes there is no consensus for the breaking design and says the RFC should use the compatible direction.
A maintainer checks whether the author intends to revise the RFC and offers help.
The author declines to implement the compatible design, but offers to investigate the original design further or wait for a future major release.
A maintainer says the project will proceed only with a compatible approach and offers to close the RFC so another author can take it up.
The author steps back from the current RFC while remaining open to future work on object normalization.
A maintainer closes the pull request.
The maintainer confirms in a comment that the RFC is closing for now.
The original feature requester thanks the author and says waiting for a future major release is acceptable while existing workarounds remain.
